And the Apostle: [[Rom 8:23|we ourselves|Nos ipsi]], he says, [[Rom 8:23|who have the firstfruits of the Spirit|primitias Spiritus habentes]].

paras.t: Et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter de Deo et creaturis, et de Christi mysteriis, et didici : quia ex infusa sapientia profecit, et scientiam acquisivit majorem. Dedique cor meum, id est, intellectum applicui, rogando Deum pro sapientia infundenda, vel investigando quædam ignota, ut scirem prudentiam, quæ est recta ratio agibilium, et docet quid et qualiter sit agendum, quid item vitandum, atque doctrinam moralem, seu legis divinæ notitiam, erroresque et stultitiam, id est, errores veritati contrarios, et stultitiam sapientiæ oppositam, volui scire, ad vitandum et reprobandum eos, qui nisi agnoscantur, non evitantur. Eadem tamen, secundum Philosophum, est scientia contrariorum. Et agnovi per experientiam in me ipso, quod in his quoque esset labor, et afflictio spiritus. Laboriosum enim est ita studere atque proficere, quia (ut ait Philosophus) ars et virtus sunt circa difficilia. Per hoc quoque, quod homo acquirit prudentiam et doctrinam, agnoscit sui ipsius errores præteritos et excessus : ex quibus afflictionem, contritionem, tristitiam concipit, et pro suis vitiis se affligit.
paras.en: [[1:16|and my mind hath contemplated many things wisely|Et mens mea contemplata est multa sapienter]], concerning God and creatures, and the mysteries of Christ, [[1:16|and I have learned|et didici]]: because he advanced by infused wisdom and acquired greater knowledge. [[1:17|And I have given my heart|Dedique cor meum]], that is, I applied my understanding, by asking God to infuse wisdom, or by investigating certain unknown things, [[1:17|to know prudence|ut scirem prudentiam]], which is right reason about things to be done [recta ratio agibilium, Aristotle's definition of prudence], and teaches what is to be done and how, and likewise what is to be avoided; [[1:17|and learning|atque doctrinam]], moral learning, that is, knowledge of the divine law; [[1:17|and errors, and folly|erroresque et stultitiam]], that is, errors contrary to truth and folly opposed to wisdom, I wished to know, in order to avoid and condemn them, since unless they are recognized they are not avoided. Yet, according to the Philosopher, the knowledge of contraries is one and the same. [[1:17|and I have perceived|Et agnovi]] by experience in myself [[1:17|that in these also there was labour, and vexation of spirit|quod in his quoque esset labor, et afflictio spiritus]]. For it is laborious to study and advance in this way, since (as the Philosopher says) art and virtue are concerned with what is difficult. Also, by the very fact that a man acquires prudence and learning, he recognizes his own past errors and excesses, from which he conceives affliction, contrition and sadness, and afflicts himself for his vices.

paras.t: Eo quod in multa sapientia, multa sit indignatio : id est, quanto quis amplius crescit in sapientia vera et salutari, tanto plus contra vitia indignatur, et eis subjacere abominatur, quia vilissimum et summe nocivum est subjici eis. Et qui addit scientiam, id est, qui crescit in morali doctrina, addit et dolorem : quia ex ea ad mærorem de suis peccatis inducitur, et mala proximorum ac mundi miserias agnoscendo, auget sibi dolorem et compassionem, fletum atque tristitiam. Iterum, Qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem, id est, damnationem sibi adauget, nisi juxta scientiam suam vivat, sicut in Evangelio loquitur Christus : Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et non præparavit, et non fecit secundum voluntatem ejus, plagis vapulabit multis. Præterea sapientia et scientia acquisitæ, frequenter inflant habentem : sicque faciunt eum promptum ad indignandum his, qui aliter agunt quam sibi placet. Quia vult reputari et honorari, idcirco indignatur eis, a quibus putat se parvi pendi. Unde ex indignatione ac impatientia incurrit dolorem, id est afflictionem interiorem, et anxietatem displicentiamque turbantem. Quibus miseriis careret, si esset humilis ac patiens, et sapientiam quæ donum est, possideret : quia, ut apostolus Jacobus testatur, Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica et modesta. Postremo, in multa sapientia, multa est indignatio : quoniam his qui multum eruditi sunt, Deus gravissime indignatur, si prave et inexemplariter conversentur.
paras.en: [[1:18|Because in much wisdom there is much indignation|Eo quod in multa sapientia, multa sit indignatio]]: that is, the more one grows in true and saving wisdom, the more one is indignant against vices and abhors being subject to them, since to be subject to them is most vile and supremely harmful. [[1:18|and he that addeth knowledge|Et qui addit scientiam]], that is, he who grows in moral learning, [[1:18|addeth also labour|addit et dolorem]] [Denis reads dolorem, "sorrow", where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "labour"]: because by it he is led to grief for his sins, and by recognizing the evils of his neighbours and the miseries of the world he increases his own sorrow and compassion, weeping and sadness. Again, he that addeth knowledge addeth also sorrow: that is, he increases his own damnation, unless he lives according to his knowledge, as Christ says in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord and prepared not himself and did not according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes|Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et non præparavit, et non fecit secundum voluntatem ejus, plagis vapulabit multis]]. Moreover, acquired wisdom and knowledge often puff up the one who has them, and so make him quick to be indignant at those who act otherwise than pleases him. Because he wants to be esteemed and honoured, he is therefore indignant at those by whom he thinks himself little regarded. Hence from indignation and impatience he incurs sorrow, that is, inward affliction, and an anxiety and displeasure that trouble him. He would be free of these miseries if he were humble and patient and possessed the wisdom that is a gift: for, as the apostle James testifies, [[Jas 3:17|the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, modest|Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica et modesta]]. Lastly, in much wisdom there is much indignation, since God is most gravely indignant with those who are very learned if they live wickedly and give no good example.

2.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI SECUNDI : DIXI ERGO IN CORDE MEO, ETC.
2.title_en: Exposition of the second chapter: I said in my heart, etc.

paras.t: Hic multipliciter Salomon docet, non felicitatem, sed vanitatem, in corporalibus bonis ac deliciis carnis consistere. Itaque in persona hominis carnalis imperitique loquens, subdit: Dixi ergo in corde meo, id est, ex quo inveni, in sapientia atque scientia esse indignationem et dolorem, non quietem et sufficientiam ac salutem. Nam et scientia hujus vitæ, est modica: et quanto quis in scientia proficit, tanto clarius cernit quantum a perfecta omnium rerum scientia distet. Propter quod dolet quod ad plenitudinem scientiæ nequit pertingere. Ideo dixi intra me: Vadam, id est, ab occupatione circa profectum sapientiæ et scientiæ abiens, pergam ad objecta carnalium deliciarum, et affluam, id est, abundanter vacabo, deliciis gulæ et luxus, et fruar bonis exterioribus, illis finaliter inhærendo. Nam fine fruimur, mediis utimur. Et vidi, id est, faciliter celeriterque pensavi, quod hoc quoque esset vanitas, id est impium et brutale, avertens mentem a Deo, et eam infimis rebus omnino immergens.
paras.en: Here Solomon teaches in many ways that not happiness but vanity lies in bodily goods and the delights of the flesh. And so, speaking in the person of a carnal and unskilled man, he goes on: [[2:1|I said in my heart|Dixi ergo in corde meo]], that is: since I have found that in wisdom and knowledge there is indignation and sorrow, not rest and sufficiency and salvation. For the knowledge of this life is slight; and the further anyone advances in knowledge, the more clearly he sees how far he is from a perfect knowledge of all things. Because of this he grieves that he cannot reach the fullness of knowledge. Therefore I said within myself: [[2:1|I will go|Vadam]], that is, leaving off my occupation with progress in wisdom and knowledge, I will betake myself to the objects of carnal delights, [[2:1|and abound|et affluam]], that is, I will give myself abundantly, [[2:1|with delights|deliciis]] of gluttony and lust, [[2:1|and enjoy good things|et fruar bonis]] outward ones, cleaving to them as to my end. For we enjoy the end, and use the means [that is, to "enjoy" (frui) is to rest in a thing for its own sake as one's end, to "use" (uti) is to refer it to something else; the distinction is Augustine's]. [[2:1|And I saw|Et vidi]], that is, I weighed easily and quickly, [[2:1|that this also was vanity|quod hoc quoque esset vanitas]], that is, a thing impious and brutish, turning the mind away from God and plunging it wholly in the lowest things.

paras.t: Risum reputavi errorem, id est, erroneum judicavi inordinato risui et ineptis ac dissolutis lætitiis locum dare; et gaudio dixi: Quid frustra deciperis? id est, delectationem carnalem illicitam reprobavi, eo quod fallax sit, et ad perpetuum trahat mœrorem. Quum enim simus in sæculo isto tanquam in exsilio et loco peregrinationis, valleque lacrimarum, ubi actibus pœnitentiæ vacare oportet, non est hic locus aut tempus risuum et jocorum, sive inanium gaudiorum; sed implere oportet quod per Joelem Dominus exhortatur, Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro, in jejunio, et fletu, et planctu. Ad Corinthios quoque scribens Paulus, docet et monet: In omnibus, inquiens, exhibeamus nosmetipsos sicut Dei ministros, in multa patientia, in tribulationibus, in angustiis, in necessitatibus, in plagis, in carceribus, in seditionibus, in laboribus, in vigiliis, in jejuniis, in castitate, in scientia, in longanimitate, in suavitate, in Spiritu Sancto, in caritate non ficta, in verbo veritatis, in virtute Dei, per arma justitiæ a dextris et a sinistris. Hinc loquitur Jeremias: Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga? Atque in Evangelio Veritas: Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia plorabitis et flebitis. Ideo scriptum est: Agite nunc, divites, plorate ululantes in miseriis quæ advenient vobis.
paras.en: [[2:2|Laughter I counted error|Risum reputavi errorem]], that is, I judged it erroneous to give place to disordered laughter and to foolish and dissolute merriment; [[2:2|and to mirth I said: Why art thou vainly deceived?|et gaudio dixi: Quid frustra deciperis?]] that is, I condemned unlawful carnal delight, because it is deceitful and drags one down to everlasting mourning. For since we are in this world as in an exile and a place of pilgrimage, and a vale of tears, where we ought to give ourselves to works of penance, this is not the place or the time for laughter and jests or for empty joys; but we must fulfil what the Lord exhorts through Joel: [[Joel 2:12|Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and mourning|Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro, in jejunio, et fletu, et planctu]]. Paul too, writing to the Corinthians, teaches and admonishes: [[2 Cor 6:4|in all things|In omnibus]], he says, [[2 Cor 6:4|let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in tribulation, in necessities, in distresses|exhibeamus nosmetipsos sicut Dei ministros, in multa patientia, in tribulationibus, in angustiis, in necessitatibus]], [[2 Cor 6:5|In stripes, in prisons, in seditions, in labours, in watchings, in fastings|in plagis, in carceribus, in seditionibus, in laboribus, in vigiliis, in jejuniis]], [[2 Cor 6:6|In chastity, in knowledge, in longsuffering, in sweetness, in the Holy Ghost, in charity unfeigned|in castitate, in scientia, in longanimitate, in suavitate, in Spiritu Sancto, in caritate non ficta]], [[2 Cor 6:7|In the word of truth, in the power of God: by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left|in verbo veritatis, in virtute Dei, per arma justitiæ a dextris et a sinistris]]. Hence Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:22|How long wilt thou be dissolute in deliciousness, O wandering daughter?|Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga?]] And in the Gospel the Truth says: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn and weep|Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia plorabitis et flebitis]]. Therefore it is written: [[Jas 5:1|Go to now, ye rich men: weep and howl in your miseries, which shall come upon you|Agite nunc, divites, plorate ululantes in miseriis quæ advenient vobis]].

paras.t: Cogitavi in corde meo, abstrahere a vino, id est ab omni potu inebriativo et delicioso, inflammativo et calido abstrahere, carnem meam, ut animum, id est intellectum meum transferrem ad sapientiam: ad quam obtinendam tanto aptior fit anima, quanto corpus a delectationibus carnalibus amplius elongatur. Qui enim amat vinum et pinguia, non erit sapiens. Unde in Job habetur: Sapientia non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium. Isaias quoque inducit: Quem, inquit, docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab uberibus. Devitaremque stultitiam, id est insipientiam et peccata, præsertim vitia carnis, in quibus ratio totaliter absorbetur, donec viderem, id est, vere cognoscerem, quid esset utile filiis hominum ad obtinendum veram salutem, quo facto opus est sub sole, id est, quibus operibus necesse sit hominem in hac vita esse intentum, si debeat salvari, numero dierum vitæ suæ, id est, si durante hac vita, in qua sola est tempus merendi ac demerendi, velit beatitudinem promereri. Et ut tandem per experientiam devenirem ad certam veritatis notitiam, feci quod subditur.
paras.en: [[2:3|I thought in my heart, to withdraw|Cogitavi in corde meo, abstrahere]] [[2:3|from wine|a vino]], that is, to withdraw from every intoxicating and delicious, inflaming and hot drink, [[2:3|my flesh|carnem meam]], [[2:3|that I might turn my mind|ut animum]], that is, my understanding, [[2:3|to wisdom|meum transferrem ad sapientiam]]: for the obtaining of which the soul becomes the more apt, the further the body is removed from carnal delights. For he that [[Prov 21:17|loveth wine, and fat things|amat vinum et pinguia]], shall not be wise [the Vulgate has non ditabitur, "shall not be rich"; Denis reads non erit sapiens]. Hence it is said in Job: wisdom is not found [[Job 28:13|in the land of them that live in delights|in terra suaviter viventium]]. Isaias too brings in: [[Is 28:9|Whom|Quem]], he says, [[Is 28:9|shall he teach knowledge|docebit Dominus scientiam]] [Denis adds Dominus, "the Lord"]? [[Is 28:9|and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab uberibus]]. [[2:3|and might avoid folly|Devitaremque stultitiam]], that is, unwisdom and sins, above all the vices of the flesh, in which reason is wholly swallowed up, [[2:3|till I might see|donec viderem]], that is, might truly know, [[2:3|what was profitable for the children of men|quid esset utile filiis hominum]] for obtaining true salvation, [[2:3|and what they ought to do under the sun|quo facto opus est sub sole]], that is, on what works a man must be intent in this life if he is to be saved, [[2:3|all the days of their life|numero dierum vitæ suæ]], that is, if, while this life lasts, in which alone is the time of meriting and demeriting, he would merit beatitude. And so that at last I might come by experience to a sure knowledge of the truth, I did what follows.

paras.t: Magnificavi opera mea, id est, per manum et industriam artificum jussi mihi fieri diversa opera magnæ excellentiæ. De quibus subjungitur: Ædificavi mihi domos. Ædificavit etenim pulcherrimum templum, pretiosissimum palatium, et domum Saltus Libani, prout tertio Regum scribitur. Et plantavi vineas in montibus; feci hortos et pomaria, et consevi, id est complantavi, ea cuncti generis arboribus, quæ apud nos poterant inveniri, et dignæ apparuerunt in regalibus pomariis stare. Exstruxi mihi piscinas aquarum, ut irrigarem silvam lignorum germinantium. Possedi servos et ancillas, multamque familiam habui; armenta quoque et magnos ovium greges, ultra omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem. Coacervavi mihi argentum et aurum, et substantias regum et provinciarum. Textus iste historicus est, et planus.
paras.en: [[2:4|I made me great works|Magnificavi opera mea]], that is, I had various works of great excellence made for me by the hand and skill of craftsmen. Of these it is added: [[2:4|I built me houses|Ædificavi mihi domos]]. For he built a most beautiful temple[[3 Kings 6:1||]], a most precious palace[[3 Kings 7:1||]], and the house of the forest of Libanus[[3 Kings 7:2||]], as is written in the third book of Kings. [[2:4|and planted vineyards|Et plantavi vineas]] on the mountains; [[2:5|I made gardens, and orchards, and set them|feci hortos et pomaria, et consevi]], that is, planted them all over, [[2:5|with trees of all kinds|ea cuncti generis arboribus]] that could be found among us and seemed worthy to stand in royal orchards. [[2:6|And I made me ponds of water, to water therewith the wood of the young trees|Exstruxi mihi piscinas aquarum, ut irrigarem silvam lignorum germinantium]]. [[2:7|I got me menservants, and maidservants, and had a great family: and herds of oxen, and great flocks of sheep, above all that were before me in Jerusalem|Possedi servos et ancillas, multamque familiam habui; armenta quoque et magnos ovium greges, ultra omnes qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem]]. [[2:8|I heaped together for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings, and provinces|Coacervavi mihi argentum et aurum, et substantias regum et provinciarum]]. This text is historical, and plain.

paras.t: Feci mihi, id est procuravi, cantores et cantatrices, ut per melodiam et cantus dulcedinem mulceretur auditus, et delicias filiorum hominum, id est objecta delectationum omnium sensuum exteriorum, in quibus major pars hominum quærit resolvi ac deliciari: qui magis vocandi sunt filii hominum, quam filii Dei, sicut in Genesi legitur de filiis Dei, filiabusque hominum. De talibus enim hominibus ait Propheta: Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent; et Paulus, Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Porro de filiis Dei, id est virtuosis hominibus, ait: Ego per omnia omnibus placeo. Scyphos et urceolos in ministerio ad vina fundenda. Et supergressus sum opibus omnes qui ante me fuerunt in Jerusalem. Sapientia quoque perseveravit mecum. Mirum quomodo inter tot carnalitates et vanitates ac curiositates, sapientia manserit secum. Sed certum, quod quam cito in mortalia corruit vitia, sapientiam quæ est donum, amiserit: quoniam sapientia illa non potest esse informis, nec sine caritate habetur. Sapientia autem informis, quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, potuit secum perseverare. Sicut et nunc sunt multi theologi et juristæ, non mediocriter docti et prompti in allegando Scripturas et documenta patrum ac jura, qui tamen sunt detestabilis vitæ.
paras.en: [[2:8|I made me|Feci mihi]], that is, I procured, [[2:8|singing men, and singing women|cantores et cantatrices]], so that the hearing might be soothed by melody and the sweetness of song, [[2:8|and the delights of the sons of men|et delicias filiorum hominum]], that is, the objects of the delights of all the outward senses, in which the greater part of men seek to relax and take their pleasure: who are rather to be called sons of men than sons of God, as we read in Genesis of the sons of God and the daughters of men[[Gen 6:2||]][[Gen 6:4||]]. For of such men the Prophet says: [[Ps 52:6|God hath scattered the bones of them that please men|Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent]] [the margin gives Ps. liii, 6; the words are Ps 52:6]; and Paul: [[Gal 1:10|If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. But of the sons of God, that is, of virtuous men, he says: [[1 Cor 10:33|in all things please all men|per omnia omnibus placeo]] [Denis: Ego, "I"]. [[2:8|cups and vessels to serve to pour out wine|Scyphos et urceolos in ministerio ad vina fundenda]]. [[2:9|And I surpassed in riches all that were before me in Jerusalem|Et supergressus sum opibus omnes qui ante me fuerunt in Jerusalem]]. [[2:9|my wisdom also remained with me|Sapientia quoque perseveravit mecum]]. It is a wonder how, amid so many carnal things, vanities and curiosities, wisdom remained with him. But it is certain that, as soon as he fell into mortal vices, he lost the wisdom which is a gift [of the Holy Ghost], since that wisdom cannot be unformed, and is not had without charity. But unformed wisdom [that is, wisdom not quickened by charity], which is a gift of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: a grace given for the good of others, not one that makes its bearer holy], could remain with him. Just as now too there are many theologians and jurists, learned in no small degree and ready in alleging the Scriptures, the teachings of the Fathers and the laws, who are nonetheless of detestable life.

paras.t: Et omnia quæ desideraverunt oculi mei, id est, ad quorum concupiscentiam incitabar per visum, non negavi eis; nec prohibui cor meum, quin omni voluptate frueretur, et oblectaret se in his quæ præparaveram. Et certissime hoc pessimum fuit, tam irrefrenate vacare libidini: et tamen fecit hoc infatuatissimus ac libidinosissimus iste, totus detestabilis factus. Propter quod justo Dei judicio permissus est cadere in idololatriæ scelera. Sed plane non sine grandi causa, permisit omnipotens Deus hominum gubernator, tantæ sapientiæ virum cadere tam extreme, sed ut omnes nos, agnoscentes virum illum sapientissimum taliter corruisse, jugiter timorati atque solliciti simus coram Altissimo, nec in sua quisquam præsumat scientia, nec sine propriæ fragilitatis consideratione præsumat alios informare, hortari, corripere. Et hanc ratus sum partem meam, id est, istud reputavi præcipuum bonum meum, si uterer labore meo, id est, structuris, culturis, et objectis ceteris deliciarum mearum ad libitum uterer: quod est frui eisdem.
paras.en: [[2:10|And whatsoever my eyes desired|Et omnia quæ desideraverunt oculi mei]], that is, the things to whose desire I was roused through sight, [[2:10|I refused them not: and I withheld not my heart from enjoying every pleasure, and delighting itself in the things which I had prepared|non negavi eis; nec prohibui cor meum, quin omni voluptate frueretur, et oblectaret se in his quæ præparaveram]]. And most certainly this was the worst of all, to give oneself so unbridledly to lust: and yet this most infatuated and most lustful man did it, and became wholly detestable. For this, by the just judgement of God, he was let fall into the crimes of idolatry. But plainly it was not without great cause that almighty God, the governor of men, allowed a man of such wisdom to fall so utterly[[3 Kings 11:4||]]; but so that all of us, knowing that this wisest of men fell in such a way, may be ever fearful and solicitous before the Most High[[Mich 6:8||]], and that no one may presume on his own knowledge, nor presume to instruct, exhort or correct others without considering his own frailty. [[2:10|and esteemed this my portion|Et hanc ratus sum partem meam]], that is, I reckoned this my chief good, [[2:10|to make use of my own labour|si uterer labore meo]], that is, if I used at my pleasure my buildings, my tillage and the other objects of my delights: which is to enjoy them.

paras.t: Quumque me convertissem ad universa opera quæ fecerant manus meæ, et ad labores in quibus frustra sudaveram, id est, quum prædicta facta mea et usum ac fruitionem eorum acutius considerassem, vidi in omnibus vanitatem, id est deceptionem, iniquitatem, inquietudinem, et afflictionem animi. Nam quamvis ad horam delectent, tamen delectatione expleta, sequuntur multa et magna incommoda, pœnitudo et remorsus, damna, diffamia, hebetudo, dyscrasia, et reatus mortis æternæ, amissio summi boni, spoliatio gratiæ, dominium principis tenebrarum, jugumque vitiorum.
paras.en: [[2:11|And when I turned myself to all the works which my hands had wrought, and to the labours wherein I had laboured in vain|Quumque me convertissem ad universa opera quæ fecerant manus meæ, et ad labores in quibus frustra sudaveram]], that is, when I had considered more keenly these deeds of mine and the use and enjoyment of them, [[2:11|I saw in all things vanity|vidi in omnibus vanitatem]], that is, deception, iniquity, restlessness, [[2:11|and vexation of mind|et afflictionem animi]]. For though they delight for an hour, yet when the delight is spent there follow many great harms: regret and remorse, losses, ill fame, dullness, dyscrasia [that is, a bad mixture of the bodily humours, ill health], and the guilt of eternal death, the loss of the highest good, the stripping away of grace, the dominion of the prince of darkness, and the yoke of vices.

paras.t: Et nihil permanere sub sole. Præcedenti dixit capitulo: Terra in æternum stat. Terra autem sub sole est. Quomodo ergo nunc ait, nihil permanere sub sole? Sub sole quoque sunt, non solum ignis, aer, aqua, tria elementa perpetua, sed et luna cum sphæra sua, quam Aristoteles posuit proximam sphæræ solis; imo et Venus atque Mercurius, secundum Ptolemæum, qui solem asserit esse in medio planetarum: quod tenetur communius, et creditur verius. Quum itaque cœlestia corpora incorruptibilia sint, quomodo nihil manet sub sole? Respondendum, quod sub sole dicitur nil manere, quia contenta sub sole subjacent mutationi secundum locum et situm, aut secundum formam et esse, sive pro parte sua, sive secundum se tota. Et quamvis quædam cœlestia corpora sint sub sole, proprie tamen dicuntur esse sub sole, quæ subjacent influentiæ solis, recipiendo peregrinas impressiones, et quantum ad generationem et corruptionem.
paras.en: [[2:11|and that nothing was lasting under the sun|Et nihil permanere sub sole]]. In the preceding chapter he said: [[Eccles 1:4|the earth standeth for ever|Terra in æternum stat]]. But the earth is under the sun. How then does he now say that nothing is lasting under the sun? Under the sun too are not only fire, air and water, three everlasting elements, but also the moon with its sphere, which Aristotle placed next to the sphere of the sun; and indeed Venus and Mercury as well, according to Ptolemy, who holds that the sun is in the midst of the planets: which is the commoner opinion and is believed the truer. Since, then, the heavenly bodies are incorruptible, how is it that nothing lasts under the sun? The answer is that nothing is said to last under the sun because the things contained under the sun are subject to change in place and position, or in form and being, whether in part or as wholes. And although certain heavenly bodies are beneath the sun, yet those things are properly said to be under the sun which are subject to the sun's influence, receiving impressions from without, and as regards generation and corruption.

paras.t: His ergo relictis, transivi, id est, mentem erexi, ad contemplandam sapientiam, id est ad considerandum dignitatem ipsius, ut eam amplecterer, erroresque et stultitiam, ut eos vitarem ac reprobarem. Quid est, inquam, homo, ut sequi possit Regem factorem suum? id est, quum homo sit carnalis, mortalis ac fragilis creatura, non videtur quod valeat suo Creatori regi sæculorum immortali, invisibili, adhærere, servire, assimilari. Istud loquitur Ecclesiastes in persona quorumdam, dicentium hominem (quum sit mortalis et corporalis) non debere nisi corporalia atque mortalia quærere, juxta illud: Quum sis mortalis, quæ sunt mortalia cura. Cujus erroris princeps fuit Simonides: quem in Ethicis Aristoteles reprobat, eo quod nobilior pars hominis, scilicet intellectus, sit immortalis, divinus, immaterialis. Ideo homo debet summe exquirere divinorum notitiam et amorem. Et quamvis non possit suo Crea[…] per Isaiam testatur, dicens, Cui assimilastis me, et adæquastis me? et rursus: Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei? nihilo minus tamen potest ei (auxiliante gratia) finaliter adhærere, reverenter servire, per contemplationem et dilectionem imitative assimilari, tanquam ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei factus. Unde in Timæo asserit Plato, quod nobis est cum diis consortium quoddam divinitatis, et parilitas nominis. In Phædone quoque testatur: Divino, immortali, et semper eodem modo se habenti enti, similis est anima.
paras.en: These things being left behind, then, [[2:12|I passed further|transivi]], that is, I raised my mind, [[2:12|to behold wisdom|ad contemplandam sapientiam]], that is, to consider its dignity, so as to embrace it, [[2:12|and errors and folly|erroresque et stultitiam]], so as to avoid and condemn them. [[2:12|What is man, said I that he can follow the King his maker?|Quid est, inquam, homo, ut sequi possit Regem factorem suum?]] That is: since man is a carnal, mortal and frail creature, it does not seem that he is able to cleave to his Creator, [[1 Tim 1:17|the king of ages, immortal, invisible|regi sæculorum immortali, invisibili]], to serve him, to be made like him. Ecclesiastes says this in the person of certain men who say that man (since he is mortal and bodily) ought to seek only bodily and mortal things, according to the saying: Since thou art mortal, care for mortal things. The chief author of this error was Simonides, whom Aristotle refutes in the Ethics, because the nobler part of man, namely the intellect, is immortal, divine, immaterial. Therefore man ought above all to seek the knowledge and love of divine things. And although he cannot […] his Creator [the text breaks off at a column end and a line seems lost: the sense is that man cannot be made equal to his Creator, as God], as he testifies through Isaias, saying: [[Is 40:25|to whom have ye likened me, or made me equal|Cui assimilastis me, et adæquastis me]]? and again: [[Is 40:18|To whom then have you likened God? or what image will you make for him?|Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei?]] nevertheless he can (by the help of grace) cleave to him as his end, serve him with reverence, and by contemplation and love be made like him by imitation, as one made to the image and likeness of God. Hence Plato asserts in the Timaeus that we have with the gods a certain fellowship of divinity and a likeness of name. In the Phaedo too he testifies: the soul is like to that which is divine, immortal, and ever the same.

paras.t: Et vidi quod tantum præcederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris: id est, intellexi quod sapientia tantum, imo et plus, præstantior est ignorantia et errore, quantum lux caligine. Inter quæ tantum interest, ut dicat Apostolus: Quæ conventio luci ad tenebras? Ideo sapientium est, oculos cordis semper ad lucem veritatis, et ad virtutum splendorem attollere; stultorum vero, in tenebris vitiorum et falsitatis caligine volutari.
paras.en: [[2:13|And I saw that wisdom excelled folly, as much as light differeth from darkness|Et vidi quod tantum præcederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris]]: that is, I understood that wisdom is as much more excellent than ignorance and error, nay more, as light than gloom. Between these the difference is so great that the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 6:14|what fellowship hath light with darkness|Quæ conventio luci ad tenebras]]? [Denis has conventio, "agreement" (as in the next verse, 6:15), for the Vulgate's societas]. Therefore it belongs to the wise always to lift the eyes of the heart to the light of truth and to the splendour of the virtues; but to fools, to wallow in the darkness of vices and the gloom of falsehood.

paras.t: Hinc sequitur: Sapientis oculi in capite ejus: quia exteriores oculos suos elevat ad cœlestia intuenda, quatenus ex illorum intuitu, ad Creatoris contemplationem, ejus interiores oculi erigantur, juxta quod in Isaia legitur: Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc. Vel, interiores oculi sapientis sunt in capite, id est in corde ipsius, hoc est in parte intellectiva, in qua sunt tres superiores animæ vires, in quibus superbenedictæ Trinitatis imago relucet: quæ vacant divinis. Rursus, Sapientis oculi sunt in capite ejus, id est in Christo, qui est caput cunctorum fidelium: in quo sapientes interiores oculos suos defigunt, juxta illud Psalmi, Oculi mei semper ad Dominum. Stultus in tenebris ambulat, id est, per devia vitiorum, ignorantias et errores graditur ad infernum. Unde in libro Proverbiorum habetur: Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem; via autem impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt. Et didici quod unus utriusque esset interitus. Quum præfatam sapientiæ eminentiam consideravi, occurrit mihi quod eodem modo mori et deficere videtur sapiens atque insipiens: quia in morte sapientis non videtur spiritus remanens magis, quam in morte insipientis; et interdum eodem periclitantur naufragio, eodem involvuntur incendio, aut uno gladio feriuntur.
paras.en: Hence there follows: [[2:14|The eyes of a wise man are in his head|Sapientis oculi in capite ejus]]: because he raises his outward eyes to gaze on heavenly things, so that from beholding them his inward eyes may be lifted up to the contemplation of the Creator, according to what we read in Isaias: [[Is 40:26|Lift up your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]]. Or: the inward eyes of the wise man are in his head, that is, in his heart, that is, in the intellective part, in which are the three higher powers of the soul [memory, understanding and will], in which the image of the superblessed Trinity shines: which are given to divine things. Again, the eyes of a wise man are in his head, that is, in Christ, who is the head of all the faithful: on whom the wise fix their inward eyes, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 24:15|My eyes are ever towards the Lord|Oculi mei semper ad Dominum]]. [[2:14|the fool walketh in darkness|Stultus in tenebris ambulat]], that is, he goes his way to hell through the byways of vices, through ignorances and errors. Hence it is said in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 4:18|the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]; [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|via autem impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt]]. [[2:14|and I learned that they were to die both alike|Et didici quod unus utriusque esset interitus]]. When I considered the aforesaid eminence of wisdom, it occurred to me that the wise man and the unwise seem to die and fail in the same way: because in the death of the wise man the spirit does not seem to remain any more than in the death of the unwise; and sometimes they are imperilled in the same shipwreck, caught up in the same fire, or struck down by one sword.

paras.t: Et dixi in corde meo, in persona hominis imperiti carnalis: Si unus et stulti et meus, qui sapiens sum, occasus, id est interitus, seu finis, erit: quid mihi prodest, quod majorem sapientiæ dedi operam, quam stultus? quum neuter nostrum habiturus sit præmium post hanc vitam, anima exsistente mortali, ut æstimant imperiti. Locutusque cum mente mea, id est intra me conferens, animadverti quod hoc quoque, scilicet ita sentire, esset vanitas, id est pessimus error.
paras.en: [[2:15|And I said in my heart|Et dixi in corde meo]], in the person of an unskilled, carnal man: [[2:15|If the death of the fool and mine|Si unus et stulti et meus]], who am wise, [[2:15|shall be one|occasus]], that is, perishing or end: [[2:15|what doth it avail me, that I have applied myself more to the study of wisdom|quid mihi prodest, quod majorem sapientiæ dedi operam]] than the fool? since neither of us will have a reward after this life, the soul being mortal, as the unskilled think. [[2:15|And speaking with my own mind|Locutusque cum mente mea]], that is, conferring within myself, [[2:15|I perceived that this also|animadverti quod hoc quoque]], namely to think thus, [[2:15|was vanity|esset vanitas]], that is, a most wicked error.

paras.t: Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter ut stulti in perpetuum: id est, diversa erit recordatio de ambobus, non conformis, quoniam sapiens in refrigerio et beatitudine erit, stultus in damnatione æterna. Aliqui vero exponunt sic: Animadverti quod hoc quoque, scilicet majorem sapientiæ operam dare, esset vanitas: loquendo in persona carnalis. Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter ut stulti: id est, amborum memoria simili modo peribit. Et futura tempora oblivione cuncta pariter operient: id est, tandem in futuris temporibus oblivioni tradentur cuncta quæ interim fiunt, ita quod erunt sicut quæ in tenebris penitus latent. Moritur doctus similiter ut indoctus. Nam, quantum ad corpus, non videtur differentia mortis, nec animæ patet egressus. Imo sapientes, docti et justi, interdum violenta morte decedunt et horribiliori quam indocti et vitiosi.
paras.en: [[2:16|For there shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool forever|Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter ut stulti in perpetuum]]: that is, the remembrance of the two will be different, not alike, since the wise man will be in refreshment[[Wis 4:7||]] and beatitude, the fool in eternal damnation. But some expound it thus: [[2:15|I perceived that this also|animadverti quod hoc quoque]], namely to give oneself more to the study of wisdom, [[2:15|was vanity|esset vanitas]]: speaking in the person of a carnal man. [[2:16|For there shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool|Non enim erit memoria sapientis similiter ut stulti]]: that is, the memory of both will perish in like manner. [[2:16|and the times to come shall cover all things together with oblivion|Et futura tempora oblivione cuncta pariter operient]]: that is, at length in times to come all things that happen meanwhile will be given over to oblivion, so that they will be like things that lie wholly hidden in darkness. [[2:16|the learned dieth in like manner as the unlearned|Moritur doctus similiter ut indoctus]]. For, as far as the body goes, no difference in death is seen, nor is the departure of the soul manifest. Indeed the wise, the learned and the just sometimes die by a violent death, and a more horrible one than the unlearned and the vicious.

paras.t: Et idcirco tæduit me vitæ meæ, propter tot mala vitæ huic annexa: me, inquam, videntem mala universa esse sub sole, id est vana atque aliquid mali pœnæ vel culpæ admixtum habentia. Quamvis enim vita sit appetibilis per se, tamen propter adversitates et pravitates annexas potest in tædium verti. Propter quod dixit Elias: Sufficit mihi, Domine; tolle (quæso) animam meam. Job quoque: Solvat Deus manum suam, et succidat me. Atque Apostolus: Supra modum, ait, gravati sumus supra virtutem, ita ut tæderet nos etiam vivere. Et cuncta vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus, id est aliquo modo afflictiva cordis, juxta expositionem inductam. Unde oravit Psalmista: Educ de custodia, id est de carcere, animam meam, ad confitendum nomini tuo: et Paulus, Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Hinc dixit et Jonas: Melius est mihi mori, quam vivere.
paras.en: [[2:17|And therefore I was weary of my life|Et idcirco tæduit me vitæ meæ]], because of so many evils joined to this life: I, I say, [[2:17|when I saw that all things under the sun are evil|videntem mala universa esse sub sole]], that is, vain, and having some evil of punishment or of guilt mixed in. For although life is desirable in itself, yet because of the adversities and wickednesses joined to it, it can be turned to weariness. Because of this Elias said: [[3 Kings 19:4|It is enough for me, Lord|Sufficit mihi, Domine]]; [[3 Kings 19:4|take away my soul|tolle (quæso) animam meam]] [Denis adds quæso, "I beseech thee"]. Job too: [[Job 6:9|let loose his hand, and cut me off|Solvat Deus manum suam, et succidat me]] [Denis: "May God let loose…"]. And the Apostle: [[2 Cor 1:8|we were pressed out of measure above our strength, so that we were weary even of life|Supra modum, ait, gravati sumus supra virtutem, ita ut tæderet nos etiam vivere]]. [[2:17|and all vanity and vexation of spirit|Et cuncta vanitatem et afflictionem spiritus]], that is, in some way afflicting to the heart, according to the exposition given. Hence the Psalmist prayed: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name|Educ de custodia, id est de carcere, animam meam, ad confitendum nomini tuo]] [Denis glosses custodia, "custody", as carcere, "prison"]; and Paul: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] Hence Jonas too said: [[Jon 4:8|It is better for me to die than to live|Melius est mihi mori, quam vivere]] [the margin gives Jon. iv, 3, where Jonas says the same in other words; Denis's wording is that of Jon 4:8].

paras.t: Consequenter ponit unum miserabile malum, quod multis contingit parentibus. Rursus detestatus sum, id est, miseram reputavi, omnem industriam, id est prudentiam meam, quam habui in congregando opes terrenas, qua sub sole studiosissime laboravi pro acquirendis divitiis, habiturus heredem post me, quem ignoro, id est, de quo nescio, utrum sapiens an stultus futurus sit, id est, quod horum duorum ei conveniet; et dominabitur in laboribus meis, quibus sudavi et sollicitus fui, id est in divitiis meis, a me laboriose adeptis. Et est quidquam tam vanum? quasi dicat: Istud est valde inane ac dolorosum. Istud quoque accidit Salomoni, cujus successor et heres Roboam, rudis et stultus fuit, et a rege Ægypti pro parte depauperatus, ut legitur tertio Regum.
paras.en: Next he sets down one wretched evil that befalls many parents. [[2:18|Again I hated|Rursus detestatus sum]], that is, I reckoned wretched, [[2:18|all my application|omnem industriam]], that is, my prudence which I had in gathering earthly wealth, [[2:18|wherewith I had earnestly laboured under the sun|qua sub sole studiosissime laboravi]] to acquire riches, [[2:18|being like to have an heir after me|habiturus heredem post me]], [[2:19|Whom I know not|quem ignoro]], that is, of whom I do not know [[2:19|whether he will be a wise man or a fool|utrum sapiens an stultus futurus sit]], that is, which of the two will be true of him; [[2:19|and he shall have rule over all my labours with which I have laboured and been solicitous|et dominabitur in laboribus meis, quibus sudavi et sollicitus fui]], that is, over my riches, laboriously gained by me. [[2:19|and is there anything so vain|Et est quidquam tam vanum]]? As if to say: this is exceedingly empty and grievous. This too happened to Solomon, whose successor and heir Roboam was rude and foolish[[3 Kings 14:21||]], and was in part impoverished by the king of Egypt[[3 Kings 14:25||]][[3 Kings 14:26||]], as we read in the third book of Kings.

paras.t: Unde cessavi a tali divitiarum collectione, renuntiavitque cor meum ultra laborare sub sole pro opibus congregandis, eo quod filii parentum taliter thesaurizantium et congregantium, bona a parentibus congregata, male consumunt, quia facile ad manus suas deveniunt, prout dictum est plenius super illud Proverbiorum: Substantia festinata minuetur; quæ autem paulatim colligitur manu, multiplicabitur.
paras.en: [[2:20|Wherefore I left off|Unde cessavi]] from such gathering of riches, [[2:20|and my heart renounced labouring anymore under the sun|renuntiavitque cor meum ultra laborare sub sole]] to heap up wealth, because the children of parents who hoard and gather in this way squander badly the goods their parents gathered, since these come easily into their hands, as was said more fully on that saying of Proverbs: [[Prov 13:11|Substance got in haste shall be diminished: but that which by little and little is gathered with the hand, shall increase|Substantia festinata minuetur; quæ autem paulatim colligitur manu, multiplicabitur]].

paras.t: Nam quum alius, id est alter aliquis, laboret in sapientia et doctrina, ut scilicet sapiens sit et doctus, et sollicitudine, id est in cura pro temporalibus rebus; homini otioso quæsita dimittit, id est, ea quæ ipse sollicite acquisivit, relinquit homini negligenti ac pigro, qui ea prodigaliter carnaliterque consumit. Et hoc ergo vanitas est et magnum malum. Vanitas est, quoniam caret fine intento a congregante, qui intendebat ea relinquere digno et sapienti successori, ac pro statu honesto per eum ducendo. Est etiam magnum malum, quia multum pœnale parenti, si eo vivente et sciente, heres suus sic devoret bona sibi a patre collata. Quod si pater ista non sciat, nec vivat dum fiunt, tamen adhuc vivens, timendo de hoc, affligebatur. Successori vero taliter consumenti bona sibi relicta, istud est magnum malum culpabile.
paras.en: [[2:21|For when a man|Nam quum alius]], that is, some other, [[2:21|laboureth in wisdom, and knowledge|laboret in sapientia et doctrina]], namely so as to be wise and learned, [[2:21|and carefulness|et sollicitudine]], that is, in care for temporal things, [[2:21|he leaveth what he hath gotten to an idle man|homini otioso quæsita dimittit]], that is, what he himself carefully acquired he leaves to a negligent and slothful man, who squanders it prodigally and carnally. [[2:21|so this also is vanity, and a great evil|Et hoc ergo vanitas est et magnum malum]]. It is vanity, because it lacks the end intended by the one who gathered, who meant to leave these things to a worthy and wise successor, and for the leading of an honourable estate by him. It is also a great evil, because it is very painful to the parent if, while he is living and knows it, his heir so devours the goods bestowed on him by his father. And if the father does not know these things, nor is alive while they happen, yet while still living he was afflicted by fearing it. But for the successor who so squanders the goods left to him, it is a great evil of guilt.

paras.t: Quid enim proderit homini cuicumque, id est, quam utilitatem consequitur homo quicumque avarus et tenax, de universo labore suo, quo pro divitiis laboravit, vel de ipsis divitiis laboriose collectis, et afflictione, id est sollicitudine et anxietate, spiritus, id est animæ suæ, qua sub sole cruciatus est propter ista terrena, quæ cum labore acquiruntur, cum timore possidentur, cum dolore et tristitia amittuntur? Cuncti dies ejus doloribus et ærumnis, id est miseris curis, malisque pœnæ et culpæ, pleni sunt: hoc est, ipsemet in diebus suis his calamitatibus adimpletur. Tempori enim adscribuntur ea, quæ fiunt in tempore, sicut ait Salvator: Sufficit diei malitia sua; et, Crastinus dies sollicitus erit sibi ipsi. Nec per noctem mente requiescit: quia in lecto corporaliter requiescens, corde sollicitatur, ne furto quid perdat, et qualiter plura adipiscatur, aut pertinentia sibi disponat. Unde asserit Dominus: Ærumnæ sæculi, et deceptio divitiarum, et circa reliqua concupiscentiæ introeuntes, suffocant verbum Dei. Et hoc, scilicet per noctem non quiescere mente, et taliter propter temporalia cruciari, nonne vanitas est? quia a vera beatitudine impedit hominem.
paras.en: [[2:22|For what profit shall a man have|Quid enim proderit homini]], any man whatever, that is, what advantage does any covetous and tight-fisted man gain, [[2:22|of all his labour|de universo labore suo]], with which he laboured for riches, or of the riches themselves laboriously gathered, [[2:22|and vexation|et afflictione]], that is, care and anxiety, [[2:22|of spirit|spiritus]], that is, of his soul, [[2:22|with which he hath been tormented under the sun|qua sub sole cruciatus est]] for the sake of these earthly things, which are acquired with labour, possessed with fear, and lost with sorrow and sadness? [[2:23|All his days are full of sorrows and miseries|Cuncti dies ejus doloribus et ærumnis]], that is, of wretched cares and of evils of punishment and of guilt: that is, he himself is filled in his days with these calamities. For the things that happen in time are ascribed to the time, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:34|Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof|Sufficit diei malitia sua]]; and: [[Matt 6:34|the morrow will be solicitous for itself|Crastinus dies sollicitus erit sibi ipsi]]. [[2:23|even in the night he doth not rest in mind|Nec per noctem mente requiescit]]: because, resting in bed in body, he is troubled in heart, lest he lose anything by theft, and how he may get more, or order what belongs to him. Hence the Lord asserts: [[Mark 4:19|the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts after other things entering in choke the word|Ærumnæ sæculi, et deceptio divitiarum, et circa reliqua concupiscentiæ introeuntes, suffocant verbum]] of God. [[2:23|and is not this|Et hoc]], namely, not to rest in mind by night, and to be tormented thus for temporal things, [[2:23|vanity|nonne vanitas est]]? For it hinders man from true beatitude.

paras.t: Nonne melius est comedere et bibere, id est rebus concessis ad competentiam uti, et ostendere animæ suæ bona de laboribus suis, id est vitam suam reficere, et se ipsum consolari ex bonis sibi collatis, ita ut habens victum, et quibus tegatur, contentus sit, et quiete vescatur? prout in Proverbiis dictum est: Divitias et paupertatem ne dederis mihi, sed tribue tantum victui meo necessaria. Unde subjungitur: Et hoc de manu Dei est: id est, ita refici et contentari, est beneficium Dei, imo et donum gratiæ ejus, ac meritorius actus, si fiat ex caritate. Quis ita vorabit, id est, tam abundantem præparationem ciborum habebit, et deliciis affluet in usu feminarum et virginum, ut ego Salomon? De cujus quotidianis cibariis et uxoribus et concubinis, tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon satis conscriptum est. Et tamen ego in talibus ita expertus, definio ac protestor, quod in ipsis non felicitas, sed vanitas sita est. Quasi dicat: Mihi in his expertissimo credendum est.
paras.en: [[2:24|Is it not better to eat and drink|Nonne melius est comedere et bibere]], that is, to use things allowed in due measure, [[2:24|and to shew his soul good things of his labours|et ostendere animæ suæ bona de laboribus suis]], that is, to refresh his life and console himself from the goods bestowed on him, so that, having food and wherewith to be covered, he may be content[[1 Tim 6:8||]], and eat in quiet? As is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 30:8|Give me neither beggary, nor riches: give me only the necessaries of life|Divitias et paupertatem ne dederis mihi, sed tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]]. Hence it is added: [[2:24|and this is from the hand of God|Et hoc de manu Dei est]]: that is, to be thus refreshed and contented is a benefit of God, nay a gift of his grace, and a meritorious act if it is done out of charity. [[2:25|Who shall so feast|Quis ita vorabit]], that is, shall have so abundant a provision of food, [[2:25|and abound with delights|et deliciis affluet]] in the use of women and maidens, [[2:25|as I|ut ego]] Solomon? Of whose daily provisions[[3 Kings 4:22||]][[3 Kings 4:23||]] and wives and concubines[[3 Kings 11:3||]] enough has been written in the third book of Kings and the second of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 9:4||]]. And yet I, so experienced in such things, declare and protest that not happiness but vanity lies in them. As if to say: I, most experienced in these things, am to be believed.

paras.t: Ideo concludendo subjungit: Homini bono in conspectu suo, id est homini vere virtuoso, dedit Deus sapientiam, id est sapidam divinorum notitiam, prout sapientia est donum, et scientiam, id est infusam notitiam de rebus creatis, quod in eis non sit finis ultimus constituendus: quæ scientia etiam donum est, et omnibus habentibus caritatem inest, sicut et cetera dona; et lætitiam, id est spiritualem consolationem, et gaudium in Spiritu Sancto, ita quod hilariter servit Deo. Peccatori autem dedit afflictionem, id est pœnales affectiones, ut sunt, timor, dolor, tristitia, conscientiæ quoque remorsus; et curam superfluam circa spiritualia, et terrena, et de vitandis periculis, seu vita productiori; ut addat terrena terrenis, et congreget ea in repositoriis suis, et tradat ei qui placuit Deo, id est, relinquat ea ita, quod (Deo sic ordinante) devolvantur in usum hominis justi, eis condigni, quamvis hoc fiat præter seu contra voluntatem et intentionem hominis cupidi, qui ea reliquit, atque ad usum alium ordinavit. Quemadmodum bona Chananæorum devenerunt in usum filiorum Israel, et opes Nabal, in usum David. Sed et hoc vanitas est, et cassa solicitudo mentis, videlicet tam sollicite congregare divitias, nec uti eisdem, sed relinquere eas his quibus non favet, neque cognovit. Itaque homini virtuoso dat Dominus consolationem internam, sicut testatur hoc ipsum expertus: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam; et alius, Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita et per Christum abundat consolatio nostra.
paras.en: Therefore, in conclusion, he adds: [[2:26|to a man that is good in his sight|Homini bono in conspectu suo]], that is, to a truly virtuous man, [[2:26|God hath given|dedit Deus]] [[2:26|wisdom|sapientiam]], that is, a savoury knowledge of divine things [sapientia, "wisdom", from sapere, "to taste"], wisdom being taken as a gift [of the Holy Ghost], [[2:26|and knowledge|et scientiam]], that is, an infused knowledge of created things, that our last end is not to be set in them: which knowledge also is a gift, and is present in all who have charity, as are the other gifts; [[2:26|and joy|et lætitiam]], that is, spiritual consolation and joy in the Holy Ghost, so that he serves God cheerfully. [[2:26|but to the sinner he hath given vexation|Peccatori autem dedit afflictionem]], that is, painful affections, such as fear, sorrow, sadness, and also remorse of conscience; [[2:26|and superfluous care|et curam superfluam]] about spiritual things and earthly ones, and about avoiding dangers, or a longer life; [[2:26|to heap up|ut addat]] earthly things to earthly, [[2:26|and to gather together|et congreget]] them in his storehouses, [[2:26|and to give it to him that hath pleased God|et tradat ei qui placuit Deo]], that is, to leave them in such a way that (God so ordaining) they pass to the use of a just man worthy of them, although this happens beside or against the will and intention of the covetous man who left them and had destined them for another use. Just as the goods of the Chanaanites came to the use of the children of Israel[[Jos 13:1||]] [the margin gives Josue xiii–xxi], and the wealth of Nabal to the use of David[[1 Kings 25:42||]]. [[2:26|but this also is vanity, and a fruitless solicitude of the mind|Sed et hoc vanitas est, et cassa solicitudo mentis]], namely, to gather riches so anxiously and not to use them, but to leave them to those whom one does not favour and has not known. And so the Lord gives inward consolation to the virtuous man, as one who had himself experienced it testifies: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]; and another: [[2 Cor 1:5|For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us: so also by Christ doth our comfort abound|Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita et per Christum abundat consolatio nostra]].
